summary: The English of 2:7–2:12 is mostly exact, but 2:9 mistranslates אֶחָד הַלֹּוֶה מִן הָאָדָם כְּלֹוֶה מִן הַמָּקוֹם as 'it is the same whether ... or' and keeps 'the righteous one' against Bartenura and Rambam, who both read God; both are patched. In 2:8 the translator took the base סוּד as 'counsel' and the English as following the Vilna variant, misreading Bartenura, who prefers סוּד 'plastered'. Many senses were filled from wrongly linked entries (place names, the verb for a noun, Qal for nifal/hifil) where the pack lists the right Jastrow or BDB entry; these are relinked. The model morphology treats the Mishnaic -ָן suffix as feminine, parses attributive nouns as construct, and has wrong analyses of בָּרוּךְ, יוֹלַדְתּוֹ, סוּד, אוּרָן, כְשָׁפִים and גַחֲלֵי.

value: מַרְבֶּה is a hifil masculine singular participle ('one who increases'). The saying runs on one pattern, מַרְבֶּה X מַרְבֶּה Y, and the English gives it as 'the more X, the more Y'; the participle carries no 'if' or 'then'.

The first five pairs set a possession against its cost (flesh and worms, property and anxiety, wives and witchcraft, maidservants and lewdness, slaves and robbery); the next four set a good against its reward (Torah and life, study and wisdom, counsel and understanding, charity and peace). The list is closed by two sentences with קָנָה, the perfect used for a general truth.

דְאָגָה (anxiety), כְשָׁפִים (sorceries, plural of כֶּשֶׁף) and זִמָּה (lewdness) are all biblical words (Prov 12:25; 2 Kgs 9:22; Lev 18:17); the pack's BDB entries for זִמָּה and עֶבֶד are proper names with the same consonants, and Jastrow's entry for רָבָה is only a cross-reference.
In קָנָה לוֹ, the preposition with suffix לוֹ is a dative of advantage ('for himself'); in לְעַצְמוֹ the noun 'bone, self' is used as the reflexive.
הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא is a noun with an article plus a participle with an article, 'the world that comes'; decisions.md fixes it as 'the world to come'.
patches.reason: The list has five negative pairs, not six (it names five); and דְאָגָה, כְשָׁפִים, זִמָּה are not post-biblical (Prov 12:25, 2 Kgs 9:22, Lev 18:17).

value: קִבֵּל (piel of קבל) is the technical verb of transmission: 'received (the tradition)'. It has no stated object in the mishnah.

אִם לָמַדְתָּ תּוֹרָה הַרְבֵּה: a conditional with the perfect (אִם plus qatal), and הַרְבֵּה, the hifil infinitive absolute of רבה, used as an adverb after the object; אַל תַּחֲזִיק is a negative command with hifil yiqtol of חזק.
חֲמִשָּׁה תַלְמִידִים הָיוּ לוֹ: possession is expressed by הָיָה plus ל ('five disciples were to him'); the following לְרַבָּן יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי repeats the owner by name.

הוּא הָיָה מוֹנֶה שִׁבְחָן and הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר: הָיָה with a participle is the habitual past ('used to enumerate', 'used to say'); the suffix -ָן in שִׁבְחָן is the Mishnaic 3rd person plural, used for masculine as for feminine referents: 'their praises'.

Each praise is a nominal clause without a verb: name, then predicate (בּוֹר סוּד ..., אַשְׁרֵי יוֹלַדְתּוֹ, חָסִיד, יְרֵא חֵטְא, מַעְיָן הַמִּתְגַּבֵּר); יְרֵא חֵטְא is a construct chain of adjective and noun.
מַכְרִיעַ אֶת כֻּלָּם: hifil participle of כרע, 'tilts the scale against them all'; the weighing is expressed by a conditional with the plural יִהְיוּ and the dual מֹאזְנַיִם, 'a pair of scales'.
patches.reason: The Mishnaic suffix -ָן is the 3rd person plural for masculine as well as feminine referents (biblical -ָם/-ָהֶם); here it refers to masculine persons, so the analysis is masculine plural.

patches.value: קִבֵּל מֵהִלֵּל וּמִשַּׁמָּאי: the English leaves the object unsaid, as in the Hebrew; the sense is 'received the tradition'. אַל תַּחֲזִיק טוֹבָה לְעַצְמְךָ: 'do not claim credit for yourself' (Bartenura: do not say 'I have learned much Torah'; he left no Scripture, Mishnah, halakhah or aggadah unlearned). The literal 'do not hold goodness for yourself' is kept in the literal line. בּוֹר סוּד: סוּד is the passive participle of סוד 'to plaster': 'a plastered cistern'. Bartenura says that this is the reading, not בּוֹר סִיד 'a cistern of lime' (the Vilna spelling), and explains 'like a cistern coated with lime'; Rambam: 'like a lined cistern that does not lose its water'. The English follows the base text as both explain it. חָסִיד: 'a pious man'; Bartenura: one who acts beyond the line of the law. יְרֵא חֵטְא: 'a fearer of sin'; Bartenura: one who is strict with himself and forbids himself permitted things for fear of sin. מַעְיָן הַמִּתְגַּבֵּר: 'a spring gathering strength': Bartenura says his heart is wide and he adds arguments and reasons from his own mind. אַבָּא שָׁאוּל אוֹמֵר מִשְּׁמוֹ: Bartenura reads 'in his name' as in the name of Rabban Yohanan; and he writes that Abba Shaul does not dispute the first teacher, but both sayings are the Rabban's, and both are true, since for knowledge and memory Rabbi Eliezer outweighs all and for sharpness and argument Rabbi Elazar son of Arach does.

patches.value: He said to them: Go out and see which is the right way that a person should cling to. Rabbi Eliezer says: A good eye. Rabbi Yehoshua says: A good companion. Rabbi Yose says: A good neighbor. Rabbi Shimon says: One who sees what is to come. Rabbi Elazar says: A good heart. He said to them: I prefer the words of Elazar son of Arach to your words, for your words are included in his words. He said to them: Go out and see which is the evil way that a person should keep far from. Rabbi Eliezer says: An evil eye. Rabbi Yehoshua says: An evil companion. Rabbi Yose says: An evil neighbor. Rabbi Shimon says: One who borrows and does not repay. One who borrows from a person is as one who borrows from the Omnipresent, blessed be He, as it is said (Psalms 37): The wicked one borrows and does not repay, but the Righteous One is gracious and gives. Rabbi Elazar says: An evil heart. He said to them: I prefer the words of Elazar son of Arach to your words, for your words are included in his words.

patches.value: עַיִן טוֹבָה / עַיִן רָעָה: a 'good eye' is contentment with what one has (Bartenura, Rambam); Rabbeinu Yonah, who is not normative, reads it as generosity. The English keeps the idiom and gives the sense here. הָרוֹאֶה אֶת הַנּוֹלָד: 'one who sees what is to come': Bartenura says he looks at what will be and weighs the loss of a commandment against its reward, and the gain of a transgression against its loss; Rambam says he reflects on the outcome of his affairs. The literal is 'one who sees that which is born'. רוֹאֶה אֲנִי: 'I prefer', literally 'I see'; Rambam says it means 'chooses and discerns'. אֶחָד הַלֹּוֶה ... כְּלֹוֶה: 'one who borrows ... is as one who borrows': the comparison makes the debt to a person a debt to God. הַמָּקוֹם: 'the Omnipresent', literally 'the Place' (decisions.md). וְצַדִּיק חוֹנֵן וְנוֹתֵן: in Psalm 37:21 this is the righteous person who gives to others; Bartenura (and Rambam) read the 'righteous one' as God, who is gracious to the lender and gives him what the borrower did not repay, so that the borrower remains a debtor to the Omnipresent. The English follows them: 'the Righteous One'. Bartenura (2:9:6) explains why the evil way is asked about separately: the opposite of every good trait is not necessarily evil, so a second question was needed.

value: The question is asked twice: אֵיזוֹהִי דֶרֶךְ יְשָׁרָה שֶׁיִּדְבַּק בָּהּ הָאָדָם and אֵיזוֹהִי דֶרֶךְ רָעָה שֶׁיִּתְרַחֵק מִמֶּנָּה הָאָדָם. אֵיזוֹהִי is 'which is' (the feminine of the Mishnaic interrogative, agreeing with דֶרֶךְ, which is feminine); שֶׁיִּדְבַּק and שֶׁיִּתְרַחֵק are relative clauses with the imperfect (qal of דבק, hitpael of רחק) of purpose or fitness.

The answers are nominal clauses in a fixed frame: name + אוֹמֵר + noun + adjective (עַיִן טוֹבָה, חָבֵר טוֹב, שָׁכֵן טוֹב, לֵב טוֹב), and the opposites with רָע/רָעָה. The adjective agrees with the noun in gender, so עַיִן, which is feminine, takes טוֹבָה and רָעָה.

הָרוֹאֶה אֶת הַנּוֹלָד: 'the one who sees the born' has a qal participle with the article and a nifal participle with the article (the object marker אֶת before it); the idiom means to see what will come to be. Its answer-partner is הַלֹּוֶה וְאֵינוֹ מְשַׁלֵּם, a participle plus a negative participial clause with אֵין and a suffix.

רוֹאֶה אֲנִי אֶת דִּבְרֵי אֶלְעָזָר ... מִדִּבְרֵיכֶם: the participle comes before the pronoun, the usual Mishnaic order ('I see'); the comparative מִן means 'rather than'. שֶׁבִּכְלָל דְּבָרָיו דִּבְרֵיכֶם is a nominal clause with a fronted prepositional phrase.

Rabbi Shimon's second saying quotes Psalm 37:21 (לֹוֶה רָשָׁע וְלֹא יְשַׁלֵּם, וְצַדִּיק חוֹנֵן וְנוֹתֵן), introduced by שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר, 'as it is said'; the verse is in biblical Hebrew with participles (חוֹנֵן, 'gracious', and נוֹתֵן, 'giving').
patches.reason: Participle before pronoun (רוֹאֶה אֲנִי, יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי) is ordinary Mishnaic order, not a mark of emphasis.
דֶרֶךְ יְשָׁרָה is noun + attributive adjective: the noun is absolute, not construct.

value: הֵם אָמְרוּ שְׁלשָׁה דְבָרִים: 'they' are the five disciples, each of whom said three things (Rabbeinu Yonah; Bartenura: three things on conduct and character, always on their lips); the three of Rabbi Eliezer follow (Bartenura counts them in 2:10:2; Rambam holds that the third, on the sages' fire, is a saying he reported from another).

יְהִי and תְּהִי are jussive and imperfect of הָיָה used as imperatives; וֶהֱוֵי is the imperative with a conjunction. The pairs וֶהֱוֵי מִתְחַמֵּם and וֶהֱוֵי זָהִיר govern a participle and an adjective: 'be warming yourself', 'be careful'.
שֶׁלֹּא תִכָּוֶה: שֶׁלֹּא with the nifal imperfect of כוה, 'that you not be burned'.

The ending -ָן in גַּחַלְתָּן, נְשִׁיכָתָן, עֲקִיצָתָן, לְחִישָׁתָן and אוּרָן (and שִׁבְחָן in 2:8) is the 3rd person plural suffix of Mishnaic Hebrew ('their'), used for masculine as for feminine referents; here it refers to the sages (חֲכָמִים).
Each of the three comparisons is a construct chain, 'the bite of a fox', 'the sting of a scorpion', 'the whisper of a saraph', in which the second member names a creature whose attack is feared.

patches.value: מָמוֹן: 'money, property' (Jastrow); the English uses 'money' to keep it apart from נְכָסִים 'property' (2:7). שֶׁאֵינָהּ יְרֻשָּׁה לָךְ: 'it is not an inheritance to you', literally 'it is not an inheritance for you': it does not pass to you from your family (Bartenura, Rabbeinu Yonah). לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם: 'for the sake of Heaven' (decisions.md); שֵׁם is Jastrow שֵׁם II 'name'.
patches.reason: The right entry for שֵׁם is in the pack.

verdicts.comment: Bartenura glosses the order 'the more wisdom, the more yeshivah'; the base text has the reverse, which Bartenura records (2:7:6). The English stands with the base text; the patch makes the relation 'records'.
The English 'a plastered cistern' renders the base reading סוּד as Bartenura reads it; only the summary, note and apparatus misread him, and are patched.
The English made the two borrowings 'the same' and left 'the righteous one' human; Bartenura reads the borrower as God's debtor and the Righteous One as God. Patched.

Rambam, like Bartenura, reads צַדִּיק חוֹנֵן וְנוֹתֵן as God repaying the lender; the English kept 'the righteous one' and lost the comparison. Patched; his other readings (contentment, foresight, 'I choose') agree with the English.
A cross-reference to Rambam's Eight Chapters; it does not bear on the English.
